One-sentence judgment: cardiovascular technologists and technicians are not about "pressing a button on a machine"; within the physician's chain of responsibility they perform or assist with cardiac and pulmonary system examinations such as electrocardiography, cardiac catheterization, and pulmonary function testing for patients, using specialized electronic test equipment and recording devices to capture interpretable waveforms or images. O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), does not mark it Bright Outlook, and gives an interest code of RIC (Realistic, Investigative, Conventional). The core boundary: examinations and interventional support must take place within the medical institution's authorization, operating standards, and the physician's chain of responsibility, and technical personnel may not diagnose, prescribe, or independently decide treatment beyond their authority; equipment operating authorization, the right to interpret examination results, and the right to sign reports are three different things.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to check the physician's order, patient identity, and examination item item by item before contacting the patient, and willing to maintain continuous observation of waveforms and vital signs in an environment with noise and several machines running at once (the O*NET work context shows 94% in continuous contact with others, 89% indoors environmentally controlled every day, and 73% considering being exact or highly accurate extremely important); you can explain the procedure clearly and reassure a patient who is nervous or uncomfortable; and you accept working to checklists, calibration records, and quality control requirements and immediately reporting abnormalities to personnel with the authority to act.

Conditions for pausing major investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop from checking the physician's order and the patient, explaining and preparing, calibrating equipment, acquiring waveforms or images, monitoring for abnormalities, and completing quality control through recording and handover; or you are unwilling to follow infection and radiation protection standards, unwilling to record artifacts and failed acquisitions truthfully, and unwilling to stop and ask when an abnormality occurs; also, do not treat experience using a home blood pressure monitor or fitness band as proof that you can independently perform cardiac catheterization or echocardiography.

Education, credentials, and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0); it usually requires vocational school training, related on-the-job experience, or an associate degree (the O*NET education survey shows 63% of respondents consider an associate or other two-year degree necessary, 13% consider a postsecondary certificate necessary, and 10% consider a high school diploma or equivalent sufficient), plus one to two years of on-the-job training (the O*NET occupation page lists 1 apprenticeship direction: Invasive Cardiovascular Technologist). In the United States, entry usually requires a related associate degree or certificate program plus clinical internship, followed by an employer competence assessment; professional certifications are offered by bodies such as Cardiovascular Credentialing International by subspecialty (such as Registered Cardiovascular Invasive Specialist, Certified Cardiographic Technician, and Certified Rhythm Analysis Technician, with 26 certifications listed on the O*NET occupation page in total), and registration, certification, and licensing requirements vary by state, institution, and subspecialty, and certification does not equal a practice license or independent interpretation authority. In mainland China, examinations and interventional support must take place within the medical institution's authorization, operating standards, and the physician's chain of responsibility, and the position requires verifying the medical institution, medical technician entry, and in-hospital authorization, and foreign certificates are not treated as directly equivalent to local authority.

The work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, examination execution (checking the physician's order and patient identity, explaining the examination and obtaining cooperation, preparing and positioning the patient, applying electrodes or probes, operating equipment to acquire waveforms or images, and adjusting parameters per procedures); second, monitoring and safety (continuously observing the electrocardiogram and vital signs during the examination, identifying artifacts and abnormalities, maintaining the sterile field and protection requirements, and immediately alerting the physician and acting per procedures when an abnormality is found); third, recording and quality control (recording patient information and examination results, completing equipment calibration and quality control records, transcribing and distributing reports for the physician to interpret, and handling and handing over abnormalities and failed acquisitions). All three share the same chain built around patient verification, equipment calibration, and traceable records.
Examination execution

Check the physician's order, patient identity, and examination item → explain to the patient and set out the points for cooperation → prepare the equipment and complete power-on self-test and calibration → position the patient and apply electrodes or probes → acquire waveforms or images and confirm signal quality → record the examination content and the patient's response
Monitoring and safety

Editorial process: monitor the patient and equipment per institutional procedures, notify the responsible team immediately when an abnormality is identified, and cooperate with safe handling and recording; the specific suspension and restoration conditions cannot be decided by a general page.

Organize the results and equipment status of this examination → complete equipment cleaning and disinfection and consumable disposal → transcribe and distribute the report for the physician to interpret → check that key values and images match the original records → register quality control and equipment maintenance items → hand over unfinished and abnormal items to the next shift or the clinical team

U.S. adjacent occupation comparison: cardiovascular technologists focus on cardiac and pulmonary examinations and interventional support, respiratory therapists focus on respiratory support, radiation therapists focus on treatment delivery, surgical technologists focus on sterility and instrument handling, and MRI/neurodiagnostic technologists focus on other examination systems; physicians separately carry diagnosis and treatment. Medical sonographers are U.S. classification 29-2032, and the Chinese name containing "diagnosis" does not make them equivalent to Chinese ultrasound physicians. Specific duties and qualifications are not interchangeable.
Core purpose

Obtain interpretable, traceable, patient-safe examination results within the institution's authorization and the physician's chain of responsibility: ensure the correct subject through patient verification and informed explanation, ensure data quality through equipment calibration and procedure compliance, and make the process reviewable through records and handover.
Main objects and basis

The objects are patients and examination requests, as well as electrocardiographs, leads and electrodes, cardiac catheterization and angiography equipment, ultrasound and imaging equipment, Holter and event recorders, pulmonary function and exercise testing equipment, vital sign monitoring and defibrillation and emergency equipment, contrast agents and sterile consumables, and examination records and image archiving systems; the basis is the physician's order and examination request, the medical institution's authorization and operating standards, aseptic technique, infection control, and radiation protection requirements, equipment calibration and quality control procedures, patient identity and information security requirements, and the applicable jurisdiction's rules on medical technician entry and scope of practice.
Core process

Checking the physician's order and the patient, explaining the examination and obtaining cooperation, preparing and calibrating equipment, positioning and applying electrodes or probes, acquiring and confirming signal quality, monitoring for abnormalities and escalating, completing quality control, recording and distributing reports, and disinfection and handover.
Main outputs

Examination records and waveform or image data that follow standards, equipment calibration and quality control records, patient verification and informed-explanation records, contrast agent and consumable use records, abnormality and disposition and escalation records, report transcription and distribution records, and equipment maintenance and handover records.
Accountable party

The BLS duties include analyzing abnormalities and diagnostic information and summarizing findings for physicians, and O*NET also lists interpreting Holter recordings; technical analysis does not equal independent medical diagnosis, prescribing, or treatment decisions, and report signing is checked against the jurisdiction and the project authority. 
In China, institutions and departments carry the corresponding quality management, and equipment, hospital infection, and protection each have their own responsibilities. Editorial suggestion: notify the responsible physician or response team promptly of patient abnormalities and act within one's own duties per institutional emergency procedures, and do not wait until after stopping the machine, retesting, or fixing equipment to report; equipment problems follow institutional procedures for safe handover or decommissioning and restoration verification, and this text grants no uniform authority to stop, repeat, or substitute examinations.
Authority and approval

In China, the medical institution's diagnosis and treatment items, personnel statutory qualifications, and actual duties must be checked; Articles 16—20 of the clinical application measures distinguish the institutional catalog, personnel competence files, and physician surgical authorization, while Articles 22/24/25 of the Physicians Law provide for registered scope of diagnosis and examination, medical certificates, and informed consent for special examinations. U.S. state licensing, employer certification, and project competence requirements are checked position by position, and foreign certifications cannot be directly applied as Chinese practice authority.
Conclusion boundaries

The waveforms, images, and examination records are analysis inputs; the BLS duties include analyzing abnormalities and diagnostic information and summarizing findings for physicians, and O*NET also lists interpreting Holter recordings; technical analysis does not equal independent medical diagnosis, prescribing, or treatment decisions, and report signing is checked against the jurisdiction and the project authority. Patient status, equipment and acquisition conditions, and record times should be documented along with the results.

Before starting, check at least six items: job duties (electrocardiography and Holter, cardiac catheterization and interventional support, echocardiography and vascular ultrasound, pulmonary function and exercise testing, or equipment and quality control management), the required education and training and certification and the actual authorized scope, the services provided and equipment configuration, infection control and radiation protection arrangements and personal protective equipment, scheduling and on-call duty and post-exposure handling procedures, and whether you are responsible for report transcription and external release.
Occupation scope

This occupation O*NET-SOC29-2031.00, ZoneThree, not marked Bright Outlook. O*NET interest RIC: R77/I72/C62/S54/E5/A0; health care 90, medical science 58, mechanical/electrical 44, and life science 39 are independent specific interest fields and are not realistic-type sub-scores or a personal admission line. 
The O*NET 2025 industry distribution for this occupation is health care and social assistance 95%, other 5%; the BLS employer types are listed separately as hospitals 77%, physicians' offices 13%, outpatient care 2%, medical and diagnostic laboratories 2%, and self-employed about 1% (rounded), and the two classifications do not substitute for each other. No one-to-one wage correspondence with a Chinese occupational sub-category has been established, and it is checked against the actual job duties.
Education and training paths

The O*NET entry-level education survey shows 63% associate or two-year degree, 13% postsecondary certificate, and 10% high school/equivalent, which is not the incumbent education distribution; the Zone Three one to two years of training is a cross-occupation description, not a required term for every position. The BLS typically requires an associate degree or certificate plus the clinical portion of the program; EKG entry may start from high school, and certificates usually take less than a year; some states require licensing, and employers may require or prefer professional certification and may also require BLS/CPR. 
In China, the medical institution's diagnosis and treatment items, personnel statutory qualifications, and actual duties must be checked; Articles 16—20 of the clinical application measures distinguish the institutional catalog, personnel competence files, and physician surgical authorization, while Articles 22/24/25 of the Physicians Law provide for registered scope of diagnosis and examination, medical certificates, and informed consent for special examinations. U.S. state licensing, employer certification, and project competence requirements are checked position by position, and foreign certifications cannot be directly applied as Chinese practice authority. The apprenticeship lists only the Invasive Cardiovascular Technologist (Nof) example, which is not current enrollment or a requirement for all entry.
Methods and tools

The O*NET technology list has 10 software skill categories, and the Hot Technologies page lists 6, among which Microsoft Office software, MEDITECH software, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Outlook, and Microsoft Word all appear in job postings at 1% or below, while JavaScript has no given proportion (data source: Lightcast 2025 U.S. job postings). On-site methods and tools are mainly electrocardiographs, leads and electrodes, cardiac catheterization, angiography, and interventional support equipment, ultrasound and imaging equipment and image archiving systems, Holter and event recorders, pulmonary function and exercise testing equipment, vital sign monitoring and defibrillation and emergency equipment, and electronic medical records and examination registration systems. Job posting demand labels indicate frequency of appearance in employer job advertisements and do not mean the institution has deployed such tools or that the position has been replaced.
Safety and work permits

The work is mainly fixed shifts in hospitals, clinics, and examination rooms, and requires long periods of standing or bending and continuous hand operation of equipment; the main demands come from high-frequency close contact with patients, patient communication and equipment operation, infection and radiation exposure for applicable procedures, and handling patient communication and equipment operation at the same time during examinations. The O*NET work context shows: 94% in continuous contact with others; 89% working very close to others (nearly touching); 89% indoors environmentally controlled every day; 84% having face-to-face discussions every day; 73% considering being exact or highly accurate extremely important; 72% facing time pressure every day; 71% wearing common protective or safety equipment every day; 66% using their hands continuously or almost continuously to operate, control, or perceive objects and tools; 55% exposed to disease or infection every day; 52% considering the consequences of errors extremely serious; 42% having extremely high responsibility for the health and safety of others; 39% exposed to radiation every day; 36% bending or twisting continuously. Operations require personal protection per infection control and radiation protection procedures and operation per equipment calibration and quality control requirements; editorial suggestion: notify the responsible physician or response team promptly of patient abnormalities and act within one's own duties per institutional emergency procedures, and do not wait until after stopping the machine, retesting, or fixing equipment to report; equipment problems follow institutional procedures for safe handover or decommissioning and restoration verification, and this text grants no uniform authority to stop, repeat, or substitute examinations. 
These proportions are U.S. survey responses rather than every position; ECG and ultrasound do not therefore all involve ionizing radiation. The O*NET noise survey shows 50% never and 15% daily, so high noise cannot be generalized as a main demand of all positions.
Training and regulatory requirements

In China, the medical institution's diagnosis and treatment items, personnel statutory qualifications, and actual duties must be checked; Articles 16—20 of the clinical application measures distinguish the institutional catalog, personnel competence files, and physician surgical authorization, while Articles 22/24/25 of the Physicians Law provide for registered scope of diagnosis and examination, medical certificates, and informed consent for special examinations. U.S. state licensing, employer certification, and project competence requirements are checked position by position, and foreign certifications cannot be directly applied as Chinese practice authority. 
The 26 linked certifications include different technical directions as well as physician specialties and physical therapy, and are not all required for technicians; this round did not check the application fees and conditions item by item.
Pay and hours

O*NET89% report regular schedules, 65% work 40 hours per week, 13% more than 40, and 22% less than 40; a regular schedule does not mean day shifts without night work, and the BLS notes that most work full time but part time is common and evenings, weekends, or overnight shifts are possible. In 2025 the U.S. median was 74310 USD/year and 35.73 USD/hour. U.S. SOC29-2031 for this occupation: about 64500 in 2025 and 66900 projected in 2035, a change of about 4% (about average), a net increase of about 2400; the average annual openings of 3400 in 2025—2035 include turnover and exit replacement and are not the average annual net increase. 
Exact occupation wage distribution for China is still insufficient evidence; the National Bureau of Statistics 2025 health and social work industry gives 146266 yuan/year for non-private and 75631 yuan/year for private, both pre-tax annual averages and multi-occupation industry background (industry_proxy), not this occupation's median, starting pay, monthly pay, or regional ranking.

Cardiovascular technologists and technicians (O*NET-SOC 29-2031.00) perform or assist with cardiac and pulmonary system examinations of patients for diagnostic, therapeutic, or research purposes, including electrocardiograms, cardiac catheterization, and pulmonary function and lung capacity tests. Daily work includes: using specialized electronic test equipment, recording devices, or laboratory instruments to perform electrocardiograms (EKG), phonocardiograms, echocardiograms, stress tests, or other cardiovascular tests to record the patient's heart activity; explaining the procedure to the patient to obtain cooperation and reduce anxiety; using electrocardiogram equipment to monitor the patient's blood pressure and heart rate during diagnostic or therapeutic procedures and notifying the physician when abnormalities occur; obtaining and recording patient identity, medical history, or examination results; monitoring the patient's comfort and safety during the examination and alerting the physician to abnormalities or changes in the patient's response; preparing and positioning the patient for the examination; attaching electrodes to the patient's chest, arms, and legs, connecting the electrocardiograph leads, and operating the machine to obtain readings; adjusting equipment and control parameters per the physician's order or established procedures; checking, testing, and maintaining cardiac equipment and performing minor repairs when necessary; supervising or training other cardiac technologists or students; comparing measurements of heart wall thickness and chamber dimensions with norms to identify abnormalities; maintaining the sterile field during surgical procedures; observing the ultrasound display and listening to signals, and recording vascular information such as blood pressure, limb volume changes, oxygen saturation, or cerebral circulation; assisting physicians in the diagnosis and treatment of cardiac or peripheral vascular conditions (such as implanting pacemakers or assisting with balloon angioplasty); assessing cardiac physiology from blood flow velocity measurements and calculating valve areas; operating diagnostic imaging equipment to produce contrast-enhanced radiographic images of the heart and cardiovascular system; observing pressure gauges, recorders, and video displays of data systems during cardiovascular imaging; injecting contrast agents into the patient's blood vessels; transcribing, entering, and distributing pathology diagnostic reports for the physician to interpret; installing 24-hour Holter monitors and event recorders, scanning and interpreting the recording strips, and reporting the results to the physician; and completing general administrative tasks such as scheduling appointments or ordering supplies and equipment. It carries responsibility for examination quality, patient safety, data traceability, and infection and radiation protection, but does not diagnose, prescribe, or independently decide treatment beyond its authority, nor does it replace the institution's management of the services provided and personnel authorization.

O*NET occupation identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 29-2031.00 Cardiovascular Technologists and Technicians, page updated in 2026, classified as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), not marked Bright Outlook. The official duties are "Conduct tests on pulmonary or cardiovascular systems of patients for diagnostic, therapeutic, or research purposes. May conduct or assist in electrocardiograms, cardiac catheterizations, pulmonary functions, lung capacity, and similar tests."; the page lists 21 tasks (10 core + 11 supplementary); the core tasks cover using specialized equipment to perform electrocardiograms, phonocardiograms, echocardiograms, stress tests, and similar examinations to record heart activity (96), explaining procedures to patients to obtain cooperation and reduce anxiety (93), using electrocardiogram equipment to monitor blood pressure and heart rate during diagnostic or therapeutic procedures and notifying the physician of abnormalities (92), obtaining and recording patient identity, medical history, and examination results (91), monitoring patient comfort and safety during the examination and alerting the physician to abnormalities or changes (90), preparing and positioning the patient for the examination (90), attaching electrodes and connecting leads and operating the electrocardiograph to obtain readings (90), adjusting equipment and control parameters per the physician's order or established procedures (87), checking, testing, and maintaining cardiac equipment with minor repairs when necessary (78), and supervising or training other cardiac technologists or students (69); the supplementary tasks include comparing heart wall thickness and chamber dimension measurements with norms to identify abnormalities (93), maintaining the sterile field during surgical procedures (93), observing the ultrasound display and listening to signals to record vascular information (92), assisting physicians in the diagnosis and treatment of cardiac or peripheral vascular conditions (91), assessing cardiac physiology from blood flow velocity measurements and calculating valve areas (91), operating diagnostic imaging equipment to produce contrast-enhanced radiographic images (91), observing pressure gauges, recorders, and data displays during imaging (90), injecting contrast agents into the patient's blood vessels (89), transcribing, entering, and distributing diagnostic reports (89), installing 24-hour Holter monitors and event recorders and scanning and interpreting the recording strips and reporting the results (79), and completing general administrative tasks such as scheduling appointments or ordering supplies and equipment (65).

U.S. wages (exact scope for this occupation): the BLS 2025 OEWS data shown by O*NET give this occupation (29-2031.00) a national median annual wage of $74,310 and a median hourly wage of $35.73; the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles for annual wages are $39,000, $47,890, $98,110, and $121,350, and the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles for hourly wages are $18.75, $23.02, $47.17, and $58.34. The median means that half of the workers earn above it and half below; it is not an entry-level wage or a starting-salary promise; the scope of practice and equipment authorization for this occupation are determined by the applicable jurisdiction and the medical institution, and wage percentiles do not represent an individual job offer either.

Exact occupation wage distribution for China is still insufficient evidence; the National Bureau of Statistics 2025 health and social work industry gives 146266 yuan/year for non-private and 75631 yuan/year for private, both pre-tax annual averages and multi-occupation industry background (industry_proxy), not this occupation's median, starting pay, monthly pay, or regional ranking.

paragraphs: This page compares cardiovascular technologists and technicians with six adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is better suited to. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupation descriptions and do not mean the job titles or qualifications are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career direction and core outputs are based on O*NET-SOC 29-2031.00 and the official descriptions of the adjacent entries (U.S. scope); the adjacent occupations listed by this evidence route are anesthesiologist assistants, radiation therapists, respiratory therapists, orthopedic surgeons (except pediatric) and pediatric surgeons, with diagnostic medical sonographers being an O*NET related occupation; practice licensing, examination interpretation authority, treatment decision authority, and report signing authority must be verified separately for each jurisdiction and medical institution authorization, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut for changing careers.

The table below compares the differences in duties and outputs between cardiovascular technologists and technicians and the adjacent directions; the basis for judging is the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required qualifications, not how similar the job titles are.

Anesthesiologist assistants take on airway and vital sign management in anesthesia and perioperative settings, usually working with an anesthesiologist in the operating room; this occupation focuses on examinations and records of the cardiac and pulmonary systems, accountable for examination quality and data traceability.

If you would rather do anesthesia and perioperative vital sign management, look first at the anesthesiologist assistant direction; if you would rather do the execution and recording of cardiac and pulmonary examinations, look first at this occupation.
Responsible for pre-anesthesia assessment and intra-anesthesia monitoring and airway management, with output mainly anesthesia records and medication records.
Anesthesiologist Assistants

Radiation therapists focus on positioning and dose delivery for therapeutic irradiation, accountable for the accurate execution of the treatment plan; this occupation focuses on the acquisition and recording of diagnostic examinations and does not carry responsibility for deciding treatment doses.

If you would rather do the positioning and delivery of radiation therapy, look first at the radiation therapist direction; if you would rather do diagnostic cardiac and pulmonary examinations, look first at this occupation.
Prepare and deliver radiation therapy plans, with output mainly treatment plans and irradiation records.
Radiation Therapists

Respiratory therapists focus mainly on respiratory support and therapeutic procedures and can adjust treatment parameters directly; this occupation focuses mainly on the acquisition and recording of examinations such as pulmonary function, with treatment decisions made by physicians.

If you would rather do respiratory support and therapeutic procedures, look first at the respiratory therapist direction; if you would rather do cardiac and pulmonary function examinations and records, look first at this occupation.
Responsible for airway management and respiratory support therapy, with output mainly treatment procedures and respiratory monitoring records.
Respiratory Therapists

Orthopedic surgeons carry diagnosis, surgical decision, and treatment responsibility, and practice requires physician qualifications and specialty training; this occupation performs examinations and records within the physician's chain of responsibility and does not make diagnostic or treatment decisions.

If you are willing to carry diagnostic and surgical decision responsibility, look first at the orthopedic surgeon direction (physician qualifications required); if you would rather carry technician responsibility in examination and recording, look first at this occupation.
Responsible for the diagnosis, surgery, and postoperative management of musculoskeletal disorders, with output mainly surgical, diagnostic, and treatment decisions.
Orthopedic Surgeons (except Pediatric)

Pediatric surgeons carry surgical and treatment decisions for child patients, and practice requires physician qualifications and specialty training; this occupation mainly performs cardiac and pulmonary examinations for adults, with the responsibility boundary at examination quality and records.

If you are willing to carry diagnostic and surgical responsibility for children, look first at the pediatric surgeon direction (physician qualifications required); if you would rather do examination execution and equipment operation, look first at this occupation.
Responsible for the diagnosis, surgery, and perioperative management of pediatric surgical conditions, with output mainly surgical, diagnostic, and treatment decisions.
Pediatric Surgeons

Diagnostic medical sonographers focus on ultrasound image acquisition and preliminary measurement, and their duties partially overlap with this occupation on imaging examinations; this occupation covers more broadly non-ultrasound examinations such as electrocardiography, Holter monitoring, catheterization support, and pulmonary function and exercise testing.

If you would rather specialize in ultrasound image acquisition and measurement, look first at the diagnostic medical sonographer direction; if you would rather cover various cardiac and pulmonary examinations such as ECG, catheterization, and pulmonary function, look first at this occupation.
Perform ultrasound examinations and acquire diagnostic images, with output mainly ultrasound images and preliminary measurement records.
Diagnostic Medical Sonographers

Conclusion: the choice of direction is based on the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required qualifications, not on how similar the names are; once the direction is set, check the target position item by item for practice and entry requirements, the executable scope of operation and equipment authorization, training and certification requirements, and scheduling and occupational exposure protection arrangements, and keep written confirmation.

entries.answer: Perform or assist with cardiac and pulmonary system examinations for patients: check the physician's order and patient identity and explain the examination to obtain cooperation; prepare and position the patient for the examination and apply electrodes or probes; use electrocardiographs and ultrasound and imaging and pulmonary function equipment to acquire waveforms or images; monitor blood pressure and heart rate and patient comfort during the examination and notify the physician of abnormalities; adjust equipment and control parameters per the physician's order or procedures; check and test and maintain cardiac equipment; assist physicians with cardiac or peripheral vascular diagnostic and treatment procedures and maintain the sterile field; record patient identity and medical history and examination results; transcribe and distribute reports for the physician to interpret; install and interpret 24-hour Holter monitors and event recorders; and complete general administrative tasks such as scheduling appointments or ordering consumables.

entries.answer: The main risks are wrong data entering the medical record from mischecking the patient or physician's order, over-trusting automatic measurements and algorithm prompts while ignoring artifacts, inadequate infection and radiation protection, uncalibrated or abnormal equipment producing uninterpretable data, performing invasive procedures or releasing reports beyond the authorized scope, and competence depreciation under procedural and technical updates; control depends on patient verification and second-person review, original waveform or image review, protection and disinfection procedures, equipment calibration and quality control records, authorized scope management, and continuing training.

entries.answer: Fit signals are maintaining attention while in close contact with patients and with several machines running at once, being willing to check the patient and equipment item by item per procedures, and being able to stop and escalate immediately when an abnormality is found; what matters is whether there are reviewable examination records, calibration and quality control records, patient verification records, and actual operating performance, not just an interest in medical technology.

In China, the medical institution's diagnosis and treatment items, personnel statutory qualifications, and actual duties must be checked; Articles 16—20 of the clinical application measures distinguish the institutional catalog, personnel competence files, and physician surgical authorization, while Articles 22/24/25 of the Physicians Law provide for registered scope of diagnosis and examination, medical certificates, and informed consent for special examinations. subject.name: Cardiovascular Technologists and Technicians
subject.summary: This page's entry corresponds to cardiovascular technologists and technicians (O*NET-SOC 29-2031.00): within the physician's chain of responsibility, performing or assisting with cardiac and pulmonary system examinations such as electrocardiography, cardiac catheterization, and pulmonary function for patients — checking the physician's order and the patient and explaining the examination to obtain cooperation, preparing and positioning the patient for the examination, applying electrodes or probes and acquiring waveforms or images with specialized equipment, monitoring blood pressure and heart rate and patient comfort during the examination and notifying the physician of abnormalities, adjusting equipment parameters per the physician's order or procedures, and completing calibration and quality control and records and transcribing and distributing reports for the physician to interpret; the work is mainly fixed shifts in examination rooms and wards (94% in continuous contact with others, 89% working very close to others, 52% considering the consequences of errors extremely serious, 39% exposed to radiation every day), and its duties do not include diagnostic and treatment decision authority, nor do they replace the institution's management of the services provided and personnel authorization.
